newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Kohl and Cardoso slap backs, crack jokes in Brazil.
newsitem.headline: Kohl and Cardoso slap backs, crack jokes in Brazil.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, speaking of personal friendship and shared ideals, on Tuesday pledged to bring their two countries closer together.

Kohl, on a 24-hour flying visit to Brasilia as part of a three-nation Latin American tour, said that in 1-1/2 hours of talks, he and the Brazilian leader had promised to keep the European Union and the Mercosur customs bloc open to the world.
They also determined to give Brazil's already significant trade and political ties with Germany a new impetus.
"We want, sooner rather than later ... to give our ties a new boost, a new dynamism," Kohl said during a ceremony at which he signed accords on technical cooperation, transport and refuse treatment.
Cardoso, breaking the solemnity of the occasion with a smile and a joke about Kohl's famous bulk, launched into a speech praising the veteran German leader as a friend and a visionary.

"I will break with protocol because I have already realised that Chancellor Kohl himself does not like to take protocol too seriously. But he does it with a lot more force than I do, because he weighs considerably more," Cardoso said.
"I must tell the Brazilian people that we decided to act together in the world ... that the relationship between Brazil and Germany is definitely a mutual priority."

Germany is the second largest foreign investor in Brazil, sporting a portfolio that amounted to $7.0 billion in 1995. It is also Brazil's third most important trading partner with some $7.0 billion in bilateral trade a year.
German diplomats said Kohl's brief stop-off, coming after a visit in 1991 and participation in the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, showed Bonn took Latin America seriously.
Kohl, who came from Argentina and was to go next to Mexico, was travelling without cabinet ministers but with a pack of German industrial heavyweights in tow.
They included Manfred Bischoff of Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG, Ferdinand Piech of car giant Volkswagen AG and Heinrich von Pierer of electronics firm Siemens AG.
While Kohl and Cardoso chatted, the businessmen were treated to a presentation on the Brazilian economy by Finance Minister Pedro Malan which participants labelled "impressive."
"We will tell them at home that Brazil is a country to invest in," Christian Roth, head of the German builders group Hauptverband der Deutschen Bauindustrie, told Reuters.
Ties between Europe's economic powerhouse and Latin America's largest economy have been traditionally tight.

Relations began with German immigration at the beginning of the 19th century. The colonists, enticed to Brazil when slavery started to decline, settled mainly in the southern states, where the climate most resembles that of Europe.
A wane in ties during and after the Second World War, when Brazil joined the Allies to fight the Nazis, was followed by a flood of investments during the 1960s and 1970s.
Since then, German firms have become major players in Brazil. There are 1,200 German companies in Sao Paulo alone.
Kohl was to meet leading figures from Brazilian commerce on Wednesday before fying to Mexico.
